title: Chemical Kinetics - Chemistry - Rate of Chemical Reactions
subject: Chemistry

questions.q: According to the definition provided in OpenStax Chemistry 2e, how is the rate of a chemical reaction generally expressed in terms of reactant or product amounts?
options: As the total mass of product produced divided by the molecular weight.
As the change in the amount of a reactant or product per unit time.
As the time required for the reaction to reach equilibrium.
As the product of the concentrations of all reactants.
questions.explain: The rate of reaction is defined as the change in the amount of a reactant or product per unit time. For reactants and products in solution, their molar concentrations are used. Source: OpenStax 12.1 Chemical Reaction Rates.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q:
Consider the following balanced reaction involving ammonia:
$$ 2NH_3(g) \rightarrow N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) $$ 
If the rate of decomposition of ammonia ($NH_3$) at a certain instant is $2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ M/s}$, what is the rate of production of hydrogen gas ($H_2$) at that same instant?
questions.explain:
According to the stoichiometry, 3 moles of $H_2$ are produced for every 2 moles of $NH_3$ consumed. The rate relationship is:
$$ -\frac{1}{2}\frac{\Delta[NH_3]}{\Delta t} = \frac{1}{3}\frac{\Delta[H_2]}{\Delta t} $$
Given the rate of decomposition (positive value) is $2.0 \times 10^{-6}$, the rate of $H_2$ production is $\frac{3}{2} \times (2.0 \times 10^{-6}) = 3.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ M/s}$. Source: OpenStax 12.1 Relative Rates of Reaction.

questions.q: In a graph plotting the concentration of a reactant versus time, what mathematical concept represents the **instantaneous rate** of the reaction at a specific time $t​$?
options: The slope of the line connecting the initial and final concentrations.
The negative of the slope of the line tangent to the curve at time $t​$.
The area under the curve from time $0​$ to $t​$.
questions.explain: The instantaneous rate at any time $t​$ is given by the negative of the slope of a straight line that is tangent to the concentration-time curve at that time. Source: OpenStax 12.1 Chemical Reaction Rates.

questions.q: When writing a rate expression for the consumption of a reactant, why is a negative sign conventionally added to the change in concentration term (e.g., $-\frac{\Delta[A]}{\Delta t}$)?
options: To indicate that the reaction is exothermic.
To make the resulting reaction rate a positive quantity, since reactant concentration decreases.
To represent the activation energy barrier.
To account for the reverse reaction occurring simultaneously.
questions.explain: Since the reactant concentration decreases as the reaction proceeds, $\Delta[A]$ is a negative quantity. Reaction rates are, by convention, positive quantities, so the negative change is multiplied by $-1$. Source: OpenStax 12.1 Chemical Reaction Rates.
